         Theon Ranches, LP, Daniel and Kathryn Voss, and D&M Davis Land and Cattle, L.P.

(Theon-Voss and D&M Davis) 1 hereby file their Post Hearing Reply Brief, respectfully urge the

Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) to recommend that the Commission approve the Applicants’

proposed Route 894, and in support thereof show as follows:


I.       INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

         Most of the parties that filed initial briefs in this proceeding advance a common concern

that the proposed 765-kV transmission line would negatively impact their land and their way of

life. With this concern in mind, many parties ask the ALJs and the Commission either to deny the

Applicants’ CCN application, or, in the case the application is approved, avoid routing the

proposed transmission line across their properties.




1
     For ease of identification Theon-Voss and D&M Davis were designated Intervenor No. 40 in this proceeding.

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                            1                  Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s
PUC Docket No. 59475                                            Post Hearing Reply Brief – Intervenor #40
         These arguments are unsurprising given that each of the 122 proposed alternative routes

affect private property and public interests. Collectively, the potential routing alternatives threaten

ranchland, farmland, family heritage, park and recreational areas, wildlife habitat, and planned or

ongoing development. The issue before the ALJs and the Commission is not whether a particular

route has impacts, but instead which route, when evaluated as a whole, best meets the criteria

established by the Legislature in the Public Utility Regulatory Act 2 and by the Public Utility

Commission of Texas (Commission) in the Commission’s Substantive Rules. 3 The record

evidence establishes that Route 894 is that “Best Meets” route.

        A number of parties briefs affirmatively support Route 894 which provides further support

for its selection as the Best Meets route. 4 Parties that challenge Route 894 generally ask the ALJs

to elevate a particular link, region, development, property, river crossing, or corridor over the

route-wide analysis that led the Applicants to select Route 894 as the Best Meets route. 5 Many of

those parties argue for one of the “Routes of Interest” identified in a map provided by the

Applicants. 6 In addition to Route 894, the “Routes of Interest” include routes 296, 392, 410, 487,

572, 891, and CCG.

        Those parties are entitled to advocate for their preferred routes; however, a showing that

Route 894 impacts a particular property, development, recreational area, wildlife habitat or river

crossing does not demonstrate that an alternative route, analyzed as a whole, better satisfies the

applicable routing criteria than Route 894.

         The Commission does not select a transmission line route based solely on the most

sympathetic link-specific critique or on the route with the greatest intervenor support. Instead, the

Commission must balance all the relevant statutory and regulatory factors, including cost, length,

habitable structures, paralleling, environmental impacts, land use, and community values. This

route-wide evaluation is especially important in this proceeding, where a solution for one

intervenor almost certainly creates a problem for another intervenor.

        Theon-Voss and D&M Davis do not ask the ALJs or the Commission to ignore the

concerns raised in other parties’ initial briefs, but instead ask that in assessing the validity of those

concerns that the Commission’s routing criteria be applied consistently under the law. If one party

argues against a route because of the route’s development or ranching impacts, then those same

development or ranching impacts should also matter for other parties, including Theon-Voss and

D&M Davis. The Applicants evaluated the various types of impacts associated with the 122

alternative routes and, after that route-wide analysis, found that Route 894 is the Best Meets route.

        Theon-Voss and D&M Davis agree with the Applicants’ recommendation and respectfully

request that the ALJs recommend Route 894 as the route that best meets the Commission’s routing

criteria. In the alternative, if the ALJs do not recommend Route 894, they should recommend a

route that avoids Links B3, F42, and F43. Specifically, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis do not oppose

routes 392, 410, and 891.

VI.       ROUTE – BEST MEETS ROUTE

          A.      The ALJs and the Commission must apply the routing criteria consistently.

          Both PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require the Commission to

apply a multi-factor holistic review of the proposed routes. 7 As former Commission Chairman

Barry Smitherman testified, the review is “not a mathematical formula” and the Commission does

not let one factor “overwhelm the other considerations in PURA and in the rules.” 8 When

discussing prudent avoidance, he explained that “[i]t’s not a math question . . . [i]t’s a balancing

of factors.” 9 This principle is relevant in this proceeding where several parties ask the ALJs and

the Commission to focus on a particular development, a particular property, or a particular Link.

          While these concerns may all be relevant, they must be analyzed through the holistic

framework established by PURA and the Commission’s rule. The record does not support a routing

analysis that protects one development by impairing another or protects one ranch by fragmenting

another. Instead, the record supports selecting a route that, after weighing the statutory and

regulatory factors as applied to the entire route, best meets those factors. The record demonstrates

that Route 894 is that Best Meets route.

          B.      Development impacts must be equitably considered across the study area.

          Several parties opposing Route 894 rely on its effect on development. In its initial brief

Whitis Land Investments (Whitis) argues that it finalized entitlements and that those “entitlements

take a significant amount of time and resources and fundamentally change the constructability and

 value of the land.” 10 Whitis further argues that its development along Link F1 warrants deeper

consideration “[w]hen viewing entitlements in conjunction with Whitis’s track record of

completing subdivisions.” 11

         Solana Intervenors (Solana) make a similar argument in their initial brief explaining that

Solana Development, LP is “the owner and developer of Solana Ranch, a large-scale master-

planned community located in Williamson and Bell Counties along the Interstate 35 corridor

between Georgetown and Temple.” 12 Solana goes on to explain that most of Solana Ranch is

“dedicated to an active development effort.” 13 In opposing Route 894, Solana argues that Route

894 “bisects the developable core of the Solana Development property and the reserved Solana

Ranch.” 14

         Theon-Voss and D&M Davis do not dispute the basic premise of these arguments.

Development impacts can be relevant to the Commission’s routing analysis, especially when a

potential route would affect areas primed for development or where preliminary-plat approvals or

other observable development steps exist. Indeed, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis demonstrated that

their properties, also located along or near the I-35 corridor north of Georgetown, have undergone

observable and measurable development steps creating additional development-related value that

would be affected by routes using Links B3, F42, and F43. 15

that Whitis and Solana ask the ALJs to apply to their own properties. If Whitis’s and Solana’s

and D&M Davis’s approved Headwaters Preliminary Plat and the Davis Ranch/City of

ALJs should apply an equitable approach when considering potential development impacts as part

of the larger route-wide analysis. Accordingly, the development arguments advanced in Whitis’s

and Solana’s initial briefs only strengthen Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s arguments related to the

development impacts on their properties.

         C.       Routes that use B3, F42, and F43 perform poorly in meeting the

                  Commission’s routing criteria.

         Theon-Voss and D&M Davis urge the ALJs to recommend approval of Route 894. If the

ALJs’ disagree with the Applicants, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis, and the many other parties that

support Route 894 17, the ALJs should not select any route that uses Links B3, F42, and F43, which

include routes 322, 366, 376, 381, 382, 910, 911, 913, 914, 915, 916, 1162, and 1164. Each of

these routes fairs materially worse as compared to Route 894 relative to the Commission’s routing

criteria.

         The record demonstrates that the routes using Links B3, F42, and F43 do not perform well

under the Commission’s routing analysis. When analyzed under a route-wide balancing of the

routing criteria, these routes would have a detrimental impact on cattle ranching operations and

development opportunities, are more expensive than many other routes, are longer than Route 894,

have more habitable structures within 500 feet of the route’s centerline, and many of these routes

would likely result in greater fragmentation than other available routes. 18

        For the foregoing reasons, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis continues to urge the ALJs to

recommend that the Commission select Route 894 as the Best Meets route in this proceeding. In

the alternative, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis do not oppose routes 392, 410, and 891, or any other

route that avoids Links B3, F42, and F43.

       Theon-Voss and D&M Davis are not addressing this issue in their reply brief.

       For the reasons discussed above, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis respectfully request that the

ALJs recommend that the Commission select Route 894 as the Best Meets route in this proceeding.

Alternatively, if the ALJs do not recommend approval of Route 894, the ALJs should reject any

route using Links B3, F42, or F43.
